facts.title: Named From Latin for Flow
facts.text: Fluorine takes its name from the mineral fluorite (calcium fluoride), whose own name comes from the Latin verb fluere, meaning 'to flow.' The mineral was used as a flux in metal smelting because it lowers the melting point of ores and helps them flow more easily. The element's connection to the word 'fluorescence' is no coincidence: glowing fluorite specimens gave that phenomenon its name in 1852.

facts.title: A Prize Won at a Deadly Cost
facts.text: Isolating pure fluorine was so dangerous that several 19th-century chemists were poisoned or killed trying, earning them the grim nickname 'fluorine martyrs.' Frenchman Henri Moissan finally succeeded in 1886 by electrolyzing potassium fluoride dissolved in liquid hydrogen fluoride at about -50 degrees Celsius. The achievement earned him the 1906 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

facts.title: The Most Reactive Element
facts.text: Fluorine is the most electronegative and most chemically reactive of all elements, attacking almost everything it touches. It can ignite materials like glass, water, asbestos, and even bricks, and it reacts explosively with hydrogen in the dark. It is one of the very few substances that can pry oxygen out of water, releasing oxygen gas and sometimes ozone.

facts.title: A Pale Yellow Gas
facts.text: At room temperature fluorine is a pale yellow-green gas with a sharp, penetrating odor, condensing to a bright yellow liquid at -188 degrees Celsius. Despite its ferocious reactivity, the pure element is rare in nature precisely because it bonds so eagerly with other atoms. Almost all fluorine on Earth exists locked safely inside minerals as fluoride compounds.

facts.title: Teflon's Slippery Secret
facts.text: The famous non-stick coating Teflon is polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), a long chain of carbon atoms wrapped in fluorine. The carbon-fluorine bond is one of the strongest single bonds in organic chemistry, which makes PTFE remarkably resistant to heat and chemical attack. It was discovered by accident in 1938 by Roy Plunkett at DuPont when a tank of gas unexpectedly polymerized into a waxy white solid.

facts.title: Strengthening Your Teeth
facts.text: Tiny amounts of fluoride ions strengthen tooth enamel by converting its mineral hydroxyapatite into a tougher, more acid-resistant form called fluorapatite. Grand Rapids, Michigan became the first city in the world to add fluoride to its public water supply in 1945, and dental cavities in children there dropped dramatically. Today fluoride toothpaste is one of the most widespread preventive health measures on the planet.

facts.title: Splitting the Atom With Fluorine
facts.text: Because fluorine has only one stable isotope and forms gaseous compounds, it is vital to the nuclear industry. Uranium is converted into uranium hexafluoride (UF6), a gas used to separate the fissile isotope uranium-235 from uranium-238 by centrifuge or diffusion. Without fluorine chemistry, enriching uranium for reactors would be far more difficult.

facts.title: Born in Dying Stars
facts.text: Astronomers long puzzled over where the universe makes fluorine, since the element is easily destroyed inside stars. Evidence now points to aging red giant stars and possibly powerful Wolf-Rayet stars and supernovae as the cosmic fluorine factories. In 2021 scientists even detected fluorine in a galaxy seen as it was over 12 billion years ago, showing the element was being forged in the early universe.

facts.title: Medicine's Imaging Workhorse
facts.text: A radioactive form of fluorine, fluorine-18, is the most widely used tracer in PET (positron emission tomography) scans. Attached to a sugar molecule called FDG, it accumulates in active tissues like tumors and lights them up for doctors. Fluorine also appears in roughly a fifth to a quarter of all modern pharmaceuticals, including the antidepressant Prozac, because adding fluorine can make drugs last longer in the body.

facts.title: A Greenhouse Gas Champion
facts.text: Sulfur hexafluoride (SF6), a dense and harmless-seeming gas used as an electrical insulator in high-voltage switchgear, is the most potent greenhouse gas known. Molecule for molecule it traps thousands of times more heat than carbon dioxide and can persist in the atmosphere for over a thousand years. This fluorine compound shows how the element's super-strong bonds can be both extraordinarily useful and an environmental concern.
